models.collectorNote: Two-stroke cars are the specialist's joy, freewheel, smoke and all. V4 96s are the usable classic; Monte Carlo and Safari rally trims are the prizes.

generations.note: The 92's 764 cc two-cylinder two-stroke made 25 hp and the body was a wind-tunnel shape before that was marketing. The 93 (1955) added a three-cylinder two-stroke and genuine rally success.

generations.name: 96 / 95 wagon
generations.note: The definitive early Saab: Erik Carlsson won the Monte Carlo Rally outright in 1962 and 1963 in a 96. From 1967 a Ford-sourced 1.5 V4 replaced the two-stroke; production passed 700,000 across the 92–96 family.

models.intro: Saab's first three decades in one line: a teardrop two-stroke shaped by aircraft engineers, evolved from the 92 through the 93 to the long-lived 96, rally winner, family staple, and the car that made front-wheel drive make sense in winter.

models.collectorNote: Turbo cars lead the market and the mythology. Rust decides values more than mileage; a documented Turbo with a solid shell is the find.

generations.note: Engines came from a Triumph-designed slant-four built by Saab in Sweden. The Combi Coupé hatchback (1974) set the template Saab kept for decades.

generations.name: 99 Turbo
generations.note: 145 hp from 2.0 litres when turbos were exotic, the template for every Saab that followed, and a Q-car landmark. The 99 line ended as the 90 in the mid-1980s.

models.intro: The bigger, safer Saab: wraparound windscreen, ignition by the handbrake, and in 1978 the 99 Turbo, one of the first production cars to make turbocharging a road-car virtue rather than a racing trick.

models.collectorNote: Classic Turbo convertibles and late three-door turbos lead values; the Carlsson and Ruby specials are the collector trims. Convertible roofs and turbo health are the inspection list.

generations.name: 900 (classic)
generations.note: Built on a heavily evolved 99 floorpan with double-wishbone front suspension and a longitudinal engine driving the front wheels. Turbo 16 models made up to 175 hp; the convertible, from 1986, became an unlikely yuppie icon. Over 900,000 classic 900s were built.

generations.name: 900 (new generation)
generations.note: GM-era car on an Opel Vectra platform, transverse engines, including a 2.5 V6, and the talladega-challenge-proven turbo fours. Competent, and the hinge point between old Saab and new.

models.intro: The Saab most people picture: the upright windscreen, the deep hatch, the turbo whistle. The 'classic' 900 ran fifteen years and made the marque; its GM-platform successor shared the name and little else.

models.collectorNote: Aeros are the appreciating Q-car buy while they last. Torque steer is part of the charm; rust and DI cassette history are the checks.

generations.name: 9000 / Aero
generations.note: The 2.3 turbo Aero (1993 on) made 225 hp through the front wheels with famously strong 50–70 mph acceleration. Hatchback (CS) and saloon (CD) bodies; over half a million built.

models.intro: Saab's big car, developed with Fiat, Lancia and Alfa Romeo on the shared Type Four programme, but characteristically Saabified, and in Aero form one of the great sleepers: mid-range punch that embarrassed period supercars.

models.collectorNote: Turbo X and Viggen are the collector poles; convertibles are the summer buy. Everything is a parts-network car now, the Saab community is the infrastructure.

generations.name: 9-3 (first generation)
generations.note: Saab claimed 1,100 changes over the 900. The Viggen, named for the fighter jet, ran a 2.3 turbo at 225 hp and taught a generation about torque steer.

generations.name: 9-3 Sport Sedan / Turbo X
generations.note: Epsilon-platform car with Saab's cockpit intact. Aero models took a 2.8 turbo V6 up to 280 hp; the 2008 Turbo X added XWD all-wheel drive and is the modern Saab to have.

models.intro: The 900's successor under GM, twice over: first a deep facelift of the old car, Viggen included, then the 2003 Sport Sedan, all-new, with the Aero V6 and the all-wheel-drive Turbo X as its peaks. NEVS briefly restarted the line in 2013.

models.collectorNote: Second-generation cars are rare and climbing; first-gen Aero estates are the value pick. As with all Saabs, the owner's club is the real parts department.

generations.name: 9-5 (first generation)
generations.note: Aero models ran the 2.3 high-output turbo at up to 260 hp. Ventilated seats, night panel, and an estate that out-sold the saloon in some markets, peak Swedish wagon logic.

generations.name: 9-5 (second generation)
generations.note: The clean-sheet flagship: Epsilon II platform, available XWD and a 300 hp 2.8 turbo V6 in Aero trim. Production ended with Saab itself after roughly 11,000 cars, instant rarity.

models.intro: The 9000's replacement and Saab's flagship for fifteen years: the thinking driver's E-Class alternative, with the Aero estate as the connoisseur's express. Its handsome 2010 successor arrived just in time for the bankruptcy, and production stayed tiny.
